items.summary: U.S. Army Helicopter pilots in the 101st Combat Aviation Brigade are evaluating a system designed to let them relieve themselves in flight. The brigade completed the Army’s first-ever helicopter test flights using the Advanced Inflight Relief Universal System , or AIRUS, at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, from Oct. 5 to 7. Aircrews from 1-101 Attack Battalion “No Mercy,” 6-101 Assault Helicopter Battalion “Eagle Assault” and 7-101 Heavy Lift Battalion “Eagle Lift” completed human-factors surveys, checked AIRUS for fit and tested its ability to let them relieve themselves in flight.

Aircrews from 1-101 Attack Battalion “No Mercy,” 6-101 Assault Helicopter Battalion “Eagle Assault” and 7-101 Heavy Lift Battalion “Eagle Lift” completed human-factors surveys, checked AIRUS for fit and tested its ability to let them relieve themselves in flight.

The brigade’s Holistic Health and Fitness , or H2F, team sought out AIRION, the aerospace medical systems company that developed AIRUS, to help reduce the number of pilots purposefully dehydrating themselves to limit the need for restroom breaks during missions.
Gena Baisa, lead dietitian for the 101st CAB H2F team, said per an Army release.

“So, we thought, how can we get a system specifically designed to allow them to use the bathroom in air so they can stay hydrated and optimize their performance?” Chief Warrant Officer 2 Collin McAllister, an AH-64 Apache pilot who tested AIRUS, said the system differs from previous systems that used bags containing coagulant, according to an Army account of the testing.
Representatives from Redstone Arsenal observed the test to provide recommendations on AIRUS’ flight suitability.
“We tested AIRUS to see its airworthiness and started with egress testing,” said Elizabeth Rhonenus, a human-factors engineer with the Aviation Flight Test Directorate, in the release.

items.summary: A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports. After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.” The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors. In response to the attack, Saudi authorities extended the closure of the airport and said schools would be moved online until Thursday.

The effect is a quantum phenomenon in which a particle can acquire a measurable phase by travelling around a magnetic flux, even though it never passes through a region where a magnetic field is present.

PRESS RELEASE — Physicists in the Department of Physics, University of Oxford, have used a hybrid quantum computer, formed by qubits and quantum oscillators, to observe the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a quantum simulation.
The paper has been published in Nature Physics.
In classical, everyday physics, the motion of a charged particle is determined locally by the electric and magnetic fields it encounters.
Quantum mechanics allows a more subtle effect.

In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle travelling around, rather than through, a region containing a magnetic field would still pick up a measurable trace of that field’s presence.
This became known as the Aharonov–Bohm effect, and it was later confirmed in experiments with real electrons.
Physicists are now interested in seeing the effect emerge in a different setting: lattice gauge theories.
These are mathematical frameworks used to describe interactions between matter and gauge fields, including important models in particle and high-energy physics.

evidenceRecords.text: Christian was part of a team behind a study that found that spending just 10 minutes relying on an AI tool significantly impairs our ability to focus and persist with difficult tasks.
A preliminary draft made waves earlier this year, and the team presented the updated, peer-reviewed paper this week at the Conference on Language Modeling.
To test how quickly people's focus and persistence plummeted, researchers designed a series of randomized controlled trials and recruited 1,222 participants online.

In the first experiment, which involved 354 participants, one group was tasked with solving 15 basic fraction problems without help, while another had ChatGPT open on the side to use for assistance or even to ask for the answer.
The group with AI access initially answered more accurately than the group without it.
Then, after 12 problems, researchers took away the AI tool.
Almost immediately, the people in that group stopped answering questions accurately.
Researchers then ran a third experiment with 201 participants and an SAT reading comprehension prompt.
The results echoed those from the fraction problems: When the AI tool was removed, persistence and accuracy dropped.
The findings backed up what anecdotes and surveys have increasingly found in recent years: An overreliance on AI for answers erodes our cognitive fitness.
When AI produces answers in seconds, we get used to that speed; anything that takes longer feels inefficient.
And relying on AI also removes what the team called "productive struggle," which can lead people to find their research strengths and passions.

Presented by the Institute of Physics (IOP), which publishes Physics World , the international award is given annually for “world-leading contributions to physics by an individual of any nationality”.
Born in 1965 in Barcelona, Spain, Cirac earned a PhD in physics from the Complutense University of Madrid in 1991.
In 2001 Cirac became director of the Max Planck Institute of Quantum Optics the US.
Cirac is best known for his work in the 1990s in which he co-developed a proposal for building a quantum computer using trapped ions with Peter Zoller from the University of Colorado at Boulder.

The “Cirac-Zoller” proposal provided an experimentally plausible route from the theoretical idea of a quantum computer to an actual machine with trapped ions remaining one of the leading quantum-computing platforms today.
He also showed how controlled quantum many-body systems can act as simulators to solve difficult problems in physics, chemistry, and materials science.

Cirac and collaborators also pioneered long-distance quantum communication, which included the idea of a quantum repeater that offers a way of distributing entanglement across distances despite losses and imperfections.
Cirac told Physics World that he is “deeply honoured” to receive the award.
“I’m very thankful to the people who have made this prize possible – it’s a team working for many years,” says Cirac.

“I am immensely grateful to all of them for the privilege of having worked together and for everything we have accomplished along the way.” Professor Cirac’s pioneering work has helped shape modern quantum information science IOP president Paul Howarth Cirac has many other honours to his name including the Wolf Prize in Physics in 2013 , the Max Planck Medal in 2018 as well as the inaugural ICTP-IBM Richard Feynman Prize in Quantum Computing.

Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops against the Picts and Scots, but a theory that he also established a military camp near Frenni Fawr hill in Wales has so far been based on folklore.
The fort was discovered by Dr Mark Merrony, a leading Roman specialist at the University of Oxford.
He heads an excavation that is bringing to life a story about Magnus Maximus, as told in the Mabinogion, a collection of medieval epic tales of myth, magic and miracles.

Merrony expressed excitement that this landscape held the only Roman military site close to where the Mabinogion places the emperor. “If Magnus Maximus was there, there must have been an army there,” he said.
“It’s such a remote area but the tale mentions the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which is where this site is.
The presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help unlock the mystery of a Mabinogion legend that has endured for nearly 1,700 years.”
In The Dream of Macsen Wledig, medieval storytellers used the emperor’s name in Welsh in recounting his rise to power.
They described how on his military manoeuvres, he pitched his camp at Frenni Fawr, the 395-metre (1,300ft) easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills.
There had been no archaeological evidence for a Roman marching camp or fort on the summit of the Frenni Fawr or below it until now.
Merrony discovered it about 2 miles (3.5km) south-west of the summit in 2024.
Satellite imagery had shown a convincing outline in an overgrown field and, shortly after visiting it, his eye was caught by a Roman tile, which turned out to be the first of many.

evidenceRecords.text: Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian "volunteers." But veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts.
Reports of Russian combat units consisting of Ukrainian prisoners of war and former service members of Ukraine's armed forces began emerging in late 2022.
Several detachments were initially formed and in August 2026, they were merged into the so-called "Ukrainian Volunteer Special Forces Brigade."
over 30 members and confirmed they are all former Ukrainian servicemen, captured by Russian forces between 2023 and 2024.

Pavel Luzin, an expert for Russian foreign policy and defense at the Center for European Policy Analysis, believes these units are an "imitation" of the Russian Volunteer Corps and the Freedom of Russia Legion — units in the Ukrainian armed forces, consisting of Russian citizens — and an attempt by Moscow to distract from the fact that these units exist in the first place.
Ukrainian intelligence services tend to agree.
"It bothers them that Russians would fight on Ukraine's side, but Ukrainians won't fight on Russia's side," Yevhen Shybalov, author and veteran of the war in Ukraine, told DW.

He added that Russian troops have never tried to hide the fact that Russian volunteer units in Ukrainian ranks were the main reason Russian forces wanted to create Ukrainian units for their own ranks.

Butkevych told DW that between 2022 and 2023, all Ukrainian prisoners of war had received offers, "more or less persistently," to join the Russian army.

In a video circulating online that appears to be of a trial in Ukraine, he also says former Ukrainian POWs in the unit were followed and guarded by mercenaries of the private Russian military company Redut.
In the same video, he also speaks of beatings and torture, and receiving monthly wages in envelopes handed out by a member of Russia's military intelligence.
Oliynyk told DW he had been given a phone, but that he was too scared to call anyone in Ukraine because it was under constant surveillance.

I don’t think that getting rid of the NDAs automatically is going to make the people who opposed these data centers be like, “Great, let’s let’s do it.

I’m in.” But I think the beginning of that conversation is, “Well, we don’t even know what the heck you’re doing, because you’ve negotiated all this stuff in secret.” So it does seem like a good first step.
Sean: The larger problem here is just a communication problem, right?

This is a problem I think that goes across the entire tech industry, but it’s especially acute now, because we’re living in the era of “going direct” and “you don’t need to talk to the media, the media is dead,” etc.
And I’m not trying to beat that horse, because we’re in the media and [we] think we’re still relevant.

But we’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them.
And that’s because, a lot of time, the [technological] ability’s not there, and in part because they’re just not explaining it well.

It’s just wild to me that we’re a year into that, and the company still doesn’t have a very good definition of it, especially considering that they released this whole multi-page PDF laying it out when they announced this, and even Tesla’s biggest fans criticized Elon Musk and Tesla for how unspecific it was.

Anthony: One of the things this has made me think about is just the narrative and this sense that for a while, it really felt like it was being pushed down our throats — this idea of, “This is inevitable, this AI-driven future, and get on board or you’re just going to be left behind.”

evidenceRecords.text: Every week there is a new model or a tool release that claims to sound human and converse like one.
However, in reality, that might not be the case.
Enterprise voice AI platform PolyAI’s CTO Shawn Wen thinks that despite the release of full-duplex models — which can speak while listening to you — voice AI doesn’t have its “ChatGPT moment” yet.
“We have reached the milestone of developing full-duplex models.
The next challenge is to make reasoning very fast, so that the models can fetch answers quickly and the conversation feels natural,” he told me on stage at the HumanX conference last month.

“I think the next stage will be slightly different because once the voice is good enough, like, and the customer is willing to engage with them for the first two or three turns, they start to build confidence, and over time, they will feel like I probably don’t have to talk to a human if the agent can solve my problem,” he said.
Alex Gay, CMO for meeting notetaker Otter, opined that speaker identification, intent capture, and typing that up with organizational knowledge is a key step for enabling automation.
The company is also working on digital twins that might represent people in meetings.
For that technology, he said it’s paramount that the output voice gives the same emotive expressions of talking to a human in a meeting.

“If you think about the meetings that you’re in right now, the best conversations that you have are where you can have debate, and strategic discussions, and when you feel like there’s a relationship that underpins it.
If you aren’t able to have that with an avatar, then it’s just a q and a chatbot,” Gay noted.
While voice AI models have improved, AI assistants often don’t understand users, or your meeting notetaker shows the wrong transcript or a summary.
